addams-settlement: Jane Addams, the American pragmatist reformer behind Chicago's Hull House, held that ethics begins in everyday social cooperation rather than abstract rules. On her view, democracy is not merely voting but 'associated living': people, especially the privileged, grow morally by sharing life with the marginalized, so a settlement house — where different classes lived and worked together — was itself a moral experiment.
aspect-perception: Wittgenstein used 'aspect perception' or 'seeing-as' for the way we can see the very same thing under different aspects — the famous duck-rabbit figure seen first as a duck, then as a rabbit. Many hold this shows perception is never raw sensation: what we see is shaped by concepts, memory, and practice. Failing to see new aspects is 'aspect blindness,' and moral vision may partly depend on it.
avicenna-floating-man: The eleventh-century philosopher Avicenna imagined a person created fully formed but suspended in empty space, blindfolded, limbs apart, with no sensory input at all. He argued such a person would still be aware that they exist. On this view, self-awareness is basic and independent of the body and the senses — an argument for the soul's distinctness that later thinkers, including Descartes, echoed.
bacon-idols: Francis Bacon argued that the mind is not a clean instrument: it systematically distorts what it observes. He called these distortions 'idols' — of the tribe (errors built into human nature itself), the cave (individual biases and upbringing), the marketplace (the slips of language), and the theater (received systems and dogmas). Scientific method, for Bacon, is largely a discipline for unseating them.
bergson-elan-vital: Henri Bergson saw life not as a machine unfolding but as a creative surge he called the élan vital — a pushing force that generates ever-new forms through time. For him, real time is 'duration': lived, flowing, qualitative change, which clock time measures only crudely. Many have found this speculative, but it made evolution a story of ongoing creation rather than mere mechanism.
birdcage-oppression: Marilyn Frye's birdcage is a picture of how oppression works. If you look at one wire of a cage, you cannot explain why the bird stays put; only the whole arrangement of wires can. Likewise, a single barrier or 'bad luck' incident seems trivial, but systematic, interlocking barriers — in work, family, law, expectations — form a cage. Oppression, on this view, is structural, not a sum of unkind acts.
death-of-the-author: In a 1967 essay, Roland Barthes declared the 'death of the author': once a text is written, the writer's intention no longer fixes what it means. A work is a 'tissue of quotations' from a shared culture, and its unity lies where readers make it. On this view there are as many readings as readers, and the creator holds no final interpretive authority.
dialectic-of-sex: Radical feminists of the 1970s, notably Shulamith Firestone and Kate Millett, argued that the division between the sexes is a fundamental structure of power, akin to class conflict — the 'dialectic of sex.' Patriarchy, on this view, is political all the way down: marriage, housework, sex, and child-rearing are sites of domination, so 'the personal is political,' and equality requires transforming family life itself, not just winning legal rights.
film-as-philosophy: Many philosophers hold that films can do philosophy, not merely illustrate it. A film can stage a thought experiment, embody an argument in its plot, or force viewers to feel the force of a problem — personal identity, free will, the good life — in a way abstract prose cannot. On this view, watching attentively can itself be a kind of thinking.
five-faces-oppression: Iris Marion Young argued that 'oppression' is not one thing but a family of injustices with five faces: exploitation (profiting from others' labor), marginalization (pushing people to the edges of society), powerlessness (denying standing and development), cultural imperialism (making one group's experience the universal standard), and violence (random, unprovoked attacks meant to humiliate). A group may suffer any face, and the faces often combine.
mencius-good-nature: The Confucian thinker Mencius taught that human nature is inclined toward goodness. Anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm — spontaneous compassion, not strategy. He held that virtue grows from four such 'sprouts': compassion, shame, deference, and the sense of right and wrong. They still need cultivation through family love, practice, and the right environment, like plants needing soil.
mill-subjection-women: John Stuart Mill's The Subjection of Women (1869) argued that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and a chief hindrance to human improvement. Custom, Mill warned, rests on a 'mass of feeling' that argument alone rarely defeats, and marriage as then constituted made one human being the legal servant of another; ending it would free the talents of half of humanity.
montaigne-skepticism: The French Renaissance essayist Montaigne stamped his books with the question 'Que sais-je?' — 'What do I know?' His skepticism holds that human judgment is unstable: customs vary wildly, senses deceive, reason contradicts itself, and book learning breeds confident error. Many read his doubt not as despair but as a practice — holding opinions loosely, testing them against experience, and resisting the arrogance of certainty.
moral-dilemmas: A moral dilemma arises when two or more moral duties bind at once and cannot both be honored — save the drowning stranger or your child, tell the truth or protect someone. Philosophers distinguish negotiable duties, which can be weighed and overridden, from non-negotiable ones, which cannot. Many hold that in genuine dilemmas whichever choice you make, you do something wrong and carry a moral remainder.
moral-particularism: Moral particularists, like Jonathan Dancy, deny that morality runs on fixed universal rules. A feature that counts for acting one way in one situation — a promise, a need — can count differently or not at all in another. Judgment, on this view, means reading each situation's particular shape rather than applying a code; critics worry this leaves too little to guide us.
pacifism: Pacifism is the view that war and violence are morally impermissible, or at least never justified. Versions differ: absolute pacifists refuse lethal force in every case; conditional or realist pacifists oppose war in principle while allowing, as a last resort, defense of the innocent. Many pacifists draw on Gandhi's nonviolence, which holds that means shape ends — violence only begets more violence.
philosophy-of-art: The philosophy of art asks what art is and what makes works of it valuable. Is artistic value beauty, emotional expression, form, or the power to reward attention over time? Can films and video games count as art? Philosophers here try to define the concept, explain how judgment works without rules, and ask why created things can matter to us at all.
relational-autonomy: Traditional pictures of autonomy celebrate the independent self: deciding alone, unencumbered by others. Feminist philosophers of 'relational autonomy' argue this picture is false to human life. On their view, people are partly constituted by their relationships — family, love, culture — so being self-governing is not escaping those ties but competently negotiating them, ideally within relationships that support one's growth rather than crush it.
self-deception: Self-deception is getting yourself to believe something you have reasons to think false — the investor ignoring the collapsing numbers, the lover denying the evident affair. It breeds a puzzle: deceiving requires intending not to know, yet the deceiver and the deceived are one person. Philosophers debate how this is possible; many favor subtler accounts, like managing your own attention, over a literally divided mind.
society-of-the-spectacle: In The Society of the Spectacle (1967), Guy Debord argued that modern life has come to be mediated by images: direct experience gives way to commodities, celebrities, and screens, and social relations become representations of relations. The spectacle is not mere advertising but a way of ruling — even rebellion can be packaged and sold back. Genuine living, he held, must be reclaimed from the image.
stakeholder-theory: Stakeholder theory answers the question 'who is a business for?' It holds that a firm's managers owe consideration to everyone with a stake in it — workers, customers, suppliers, the community — not only the stockholders. Its rival, stockholder theory, holds the corporation's sole responsibility is to maximize shareholder profit within the law. On the stakeholder view, treating employees as expendable cogs is not just bad strategy but a wrong.
tillich-ground-of-being: The theologian Paul Tillich held that God is not a being among beings — not the biggest thing in the universe — but 'the ground of being' itself: what everything else rests on. Correspondingly, faith is not believing doubtful propositions but 'ultimate concern': what you stake your whole self on. Misplacing that ultimacy on something preliminary, he warned, is idolatry.
uncanny-valley: The robotics pioneer Masahiro Mori observed that as machines look more human, our liking rises — until the point where they are almost, but not quite, human. There affinity plunges into revulsion: the moving corpse-like face, the stiff smile. He called this dip the 'uncanny valley,' and he speculated hopefully that well-made robots might cross it, even coming to carry a kind of buddha-nature.
xunzi-bad-nature: The Confucian philosopher Xunzi argued that human nature is bad: left to itself, it follows desire toward conflict and disorder. Unlike Mencius, he located goodness not in innate sprouts but in deliberate effort — ritual (li), righteousness, teachers, and institutions that reshape feeling itself. On this view, morality is an artificial achievement, cultivated generation by generation, not a birthright. Many later Legalists radicalized his pessimism into rule by sanction.
